title: What is a sealed class/interface, what are the `permits` rules, and what must permitted subclasses be (`final`/`sealed`/`non-sealed`)?
shortTitle: Sealed classes/interfaces: what they are, the `permits` rules, and what permitted subclasses must be
keyPoints: A sealed class or interface uses `sealed` and `permits` to name exactly which types may directly extend or implement it.
Each permitted subclass must be declared `final` (no further extension), `sealed` (continues the restriction), or `non-sealed` (reopens the hierarchy).
The `permits` clause can be omitted when all permitted subtypes are in the same source file, and the compiler infers the set.
Records are implicitly `final`, so they satisfy the permitted-subtype rule automatically.
All permitted subtypes must be in the same module (or same package on the classpath).
The compiler records the permitted set in the `PermittedSubclasses` class-file attribute, and the JVM re-validates at load time.
Sealed types enable exhaustive `switch` and pattern matching: the compiler verifies every permitted case is handled.

s1_definition.oneliner: A sealed type uses `permits` to name exactly which types may directly extend it, and each permitted subtype must be `final`, `sealed`, or `non-sealed`.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **`sealed` modifier** – restricts which classes or interfaces may extend or implement the type, standardised in Java 17.
- **`permits` clause** – lists the exact set of allowed direct subtypes by name; can be omitted when all subtypes are in the same source file.
- **Subtype modifiers** – every permitted subtype must be `final` (ends the branch), `sealed` (continues restriction with its own permits), or `non-sealed` (reopens for unrestricted extension).
- **Records** – implicitly `final`, so they satisfy the rule automatically without an extra modifier.
- **Same-module rule** – all permitted subtypes must be in the same module as the sealed type (or same package on the classpath).
- **Class-file attribute** – the compiler writes the permitted set into `PermittedSubclasses`, and the JVM validates at load time.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine National Bank of India defines the concept of an "Account" and declares by policy that only three specific products may ever be a kind of Account: Savings, Current, and Loan. Head office writes this list on an official circular. Each listed product must then state its own policy: it is either a final product that cannot be sub-divided, a further sealed product that permits only its own named variants, or an open product that any branch may extend freely.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│        Sealed Hierarchy Structure            │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│                                             │
│  sealed interface Account                   │
│      permits Savings, Loan, Partner         │
│         │                                   │
│         ├── final Savings                   │
│         │   └── (no further extension)      │
│         │                                   │
│         ├── sealed Loan                     │
│         │   permits HomeLoan, CarLoan       │
│         │   ├── final HomeLoan              │
│         │   └── final CarLoan               │
│         │                                   │
│         └── non-sealed Partner              │
│             └── (anyone can extend)         │
│                 ├── WalletProduct            │
│                 └── InsuranceProduct         │
│                                             │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  Exhaustive switch:                         │
│  switch (account) {                         │
│      case Savings s  -> ...                 │
│      case Loan l     -> ...  // covers      │
│      case Partner p  -> ...  // HomeLoan    │
│  }  // No default needed                    │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
A sealed class or interface, standardised in Java 17, restricts which other types may extend or implement it. You declare it with the `sealed` modifier and a `permits` clause that names the exact set of allowed direct subtypes. Any other type trying to extend it is a compile error. This gives the author precise, compiler-enforced control over the inheritance hierarchy.

The `permits` rules are strict. Listed subtypes must be accessible, must directly extend the sealed type, and must be in the same module (or same package on the classpath). You can omit the `permits` clause when all subtypes are in the same source file, and the compiler infers the set.

The most important rule is what each permitted subclass must be. `final` means the branch ends with no further extension. `sealed` means it continues the restriction with its own `permits` list. `non-sealed` means it deliberately reopens the hierarchy for unrestricted extension. Records satisfy the rule automatically because they are implicitly `final`. Omitting all three modifiers is a compile error.

In a banking project at National Bank of India, Pankaj models account products as a sealed `Account` interface permitting savings, current, and loan. Savings and current are final leaves, loan is itself sealed with home loan and car loan, and a partner product is non-sealed for third-party extensions. The real payoff is exhaustiveness: the fee calculator switches over the account type with no default branch, and the compiler guarantees every case is covered. If someone adds a new product but forgets to handle it, the build fails immediately.

Remember one sentence: a sealed type uses `permits` to name its allowed subtypes, each of which must be `final`, `sealed`, or `non-sealed`, giving the compiler a closed set for exhaustive pattern matching.
